stories.headline: Vietnam braces for 700 mm deluge as back-to-back floods raise landslide alarm
stories.ticker: **Central Vietnam** is bearing the full force of its **second consecutive flood emergency** this week, with the National Hydro-Meteorological Centre warning of **up to 700 mm of rainfall** between 27 and 30 November across six provinces from Hue to Khanh Hoa. /// Today's **384 mm in 24 hours** is **unprecedented - ranked #1 in 87 years since 1940** for this date, against a seasonal norm of just 6.9 mm. /// Rivers from Quang Tri to Dak Lak are forecast to reach **flood warning levels** by 29 November, with **intense downpours exceeding 100 mm within three hours** already triggering flash floods and landslides in the Central Highlands. /// Over the **past 28 days, six anomalously wet days** have produced a cumulative **200.8 mm**, against an expected 5 mm. /// A warming climate has seen **p90 extreme-rain days rise from 3 to 5** per season since the 1980s, amplifying every monsoon surge.
stories.voice_script: In central Vietnam, Hue City and Da Nang are bracing tonight for the second consecutive flood emergency of the week, with up to 700 mm of rain forecast by Sunday. Today's peak of 384 millimetres in a single 24-hour period is the highest ever recorded here on this date - ranked number one in 87 years of ERA5 data back to 1940. Coastal gusts approaching 70 kilometres per hour are compounding the flood risk along Da Nang's shoreline, disrupting flights and closing beach roads. In the Central Highlands, six of the past 28 days have been anomalously wet, delivering 200 millimetres where just five millimetres is the climatological norm. Climate science links this ferocity directly to warming seas: extreme-rain days here have risen from three to five per season since the 1980s, increasing the flood toll year on year.

beats.title: Emergency alerts across six provinces as 700 mm looms
beats.text: Vietnam's National Centre for Hydro-Meteorological Forecasting has placed six localities on high alert from Hue to Khanh Hoa as the second wave of intense rainfall in a week bears down on central Vietnam. Forecasters warn of downpours exceeding 100 mm within three hours, with river levels from Quang Tri to Dak Lak expected to reach official flood warning thresholds by 29 November. Widespread inundation, flash floods and landslides in mountainous areas are considered highly likely.

beats.title: Six anomalous rain days in 28 - a relentless November soaking
beats.text: Over the past 28 days, six days have recorded anomalously heavy rainfall at the ECMWF model focus point, accumulating 200.8 mm against an expected seasonal total of just 5 mm for the same period. The 14-day total stands at 97.9 mm, nearly 20 times the climatological norm of 5 mm per fortnight. This persistence has saturated soils and swollen rivers to such a degree that any fresh downpour now converts almost immediately to dangerous surface run-off.

beats.title: Unprecedented: #1 rainfall event for this date in 87 years
beats.text: Today's 24-hour total of 384 mm ranks first in ERA5 records extending back to 1940 - a dataset spanning 87 years - for this precise calendar date at this location. The seasonal climatological norm is a mere 6.9 mm per day, placing this event at the 99.4th percentile. No comparable rainfall event has ever been modelled or measured here on 27 November throughout the entire satellite and reanalysis era.

beats.title: Warming seas turbocharge Vietnam's wet season extremes
beats.text: Local seasonal temperatures in central Vietnam have risen by 0.91 °C since the 1940-1979 baseline period. More significantly, the frequency of daily rainfall exceeding the 90th percentile has increased from three occurrences per season in the pre-warming era (1940-1979) to five in the modern period (1986-2025). Warmer sea-surface temperatures in the South China Sea provide additional moisture to cold-air interactions, systematically intensifying the rainfall events that make Vietnam's autumn flood season increasingly dangerous.

stories.headline: Siberia's winter vanishes: 28 days of record heat smash a 100-year barrier
stories.ticker: Across **Russia's West Siberian Plain**, an extraordinary atmospheric block has now delivered **28 consecutive anomalously warm days** - the full rolling month - ranking this event **#1 in 87 years since 1940**. /// The temperature anomaly has reached **+26.8 °C above the late-November norm** of -25.6 °C, with the actual air temperature sitting at just -2.8 °C in a region where -20 °C nights are climatologically routine. /// Omsk, Novosibirsk and Krasnoyarsk have recorded **not a single minus-20 °C night this season**, something that has never happened before in instrumental records. /// A powerful **Arctic anticyclone has locked the jet stream northward** for an entire month, pushing warm south-westerly air deep into Siberia and **delaying the onset of winter by at least four weeks**. /// Climate warming of **+0.91 °C locally since the 1940s** and tripling of blocking-anticyclone events are loading the dice for exactly these runaway heat domes.
stories.voice_script: Across Russia's West Siberian Plain, the city of Omsk is recording temperatures more than 26 degrees above normal - the most extreme warm anomaly here in 87 years of records. In Novosibirsk, the mercury sits at minus 2.8 degrees Celsius when it should be closer to minus 25, leaving streets snow-free and rivers unfrozen well into late November. Every single one of the last 28 days has been anomalously warm across the central West Siberian Plain, a full rolling month of heat that has no precedent in ERA5 records since 1940. A dominant Arctic anticyclone stretching from Greenland to the Kara Sea has blocked the westerly flow entirely, funnelling warm south-westerly air across Siberia for an entire month. Scientists note that local warming of nearly one degree since the 1940s has dramatically amplified blocking events, making these Siberian heat domes far more severe and persistent than in past decades.

beats.title: No minus-20 °C nights - Siberia's winter still absent at month's end
beats.text: As November draws to a close, the cities of Omsk, Novosibirsk and Krasnoyarsk have still not registered a single minus-20 degrees Celsius night - a threshold that is climatologically routine by early November across this region. Russian meteorologists report rain falling instead of snow, with only patchy, fragmentary snow cover. The warm air mass is forecast to persist at least until 28 November, sustained by a blocking anticyclone over the Arctic that is showing no signs of breaking down.

beats.title: A full rolling month: 28 of 28 days continuously above normal
beats.text: The ERA5 persistence statistics are stark: every single one of the last 28 days has been anomalously warm at the ERA5 focus point centred over the West Siberian Plain at 64.5 °N, 93.5 °E. The 28-day precipitation total stands at 36.8 mm, more than seven times the expected 5 mm for the period - indicating that unusually mild, moist Atlantic air has dominated continuously. This is the longest unbroken warm spell recorded at this location in the entire ERA5 archive dating to 1940.

beats.title: #1 in 87 years: the most extreme November anomaly on record
beats.text: The current temperature anomaly of +26.8 °C above the 1991-2020 seasonal norm of -25.6 °C is unprecedented in ERA5 records spanning 87 years from 1940 to the present. It sits at the 99.4th percentile - the absolute top of the distribution. Regional media in Novosibirsk describe this as the most unusual November in almost 100 years of instrumental observation, and local forecasters say the November 2026 season will rank in the top three warmest on record for the Novosibirsk region at minimum.

beats.title: Arctic amplification is rewriting the Siberian winter calendar
beats.text: The local seasonal warming shift of +0.91 °C since the 1940-1979 baseline period underpins a profound change in Siberia's atmospheric circulation. Research on West Siberian blocking events shows that a powerful high-pressure ridge over the Arctic, combined with southerly heat advection, can deliver sustained warm-air intrusions of this type. While the frequency of p90 exceedances has not changed dramatically at this precise grid point, the absolute magnitude of anomalies is growing because the background temperature has risen, making each blocking event more extreme than its historical predecessor.

stories.kicker: BREAKING WEATHER · WESTERN AND CENTRAL MEXICO
stories.headline: Mexico's first winter storm plunges Jalisco into an 87-year record cold snap
stories.ticker: **Mexico** is in the grip of its **first winter storm of the 2026-2027 season**, with Cold Front No. 8 driving an **Arctic air mass deep into western and central states** - bringing temperatures as low as **-10 °C**, possible **snow and sleet in the mountains of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán**, and **torrential rain in Guerrero and Michoacán today**. /// The temperature anomaly of **-8.3 °C below the late-November norm** ranks as **unprecedented - #1 in 87 years since 1940** for this date in the region, against a seasonal normal of +19.6 °C. /// Every one of the **last 28 days has been anomalously cold**, confirming this as the most persistent cold deviation on record for November. /// **Wind gusts of up to 100 km/h** and 80.9 mm of rain in 24 hours are compounding the impact across mountain states. /// Despite a background warming of **+1.19 °C since the 1940s**, rare polar outbreaks remain dangerous when Arctic blocking sends cold air this far south.
stories.voice_script: In Mexico's western state of Jalisco, the first winter storm of the season has brought an unprecedented cold anomaly of minus 8.3 degrees, the most extreme cold deviation here in 87 years of records. Mountain communities above 1,500 metres in Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán are bracing for snow and sleet tonight as the Arctic air mass pushes temperatures to minus 10 Celsius on the highest ridges. Mexico's national weather agency CONAGUA is warning of wind gusts up to 100 kilometres per hour and torrential rain in Michoacán and Guerrero, with intense rainfall also affecting Sinaloa, Nayarit and Colima. 80.9 millimetres of rain has fallen in 24 hours across the Michoacán and Guerrero mountains, raising the risk of flash floods and debris flows on roads already saturated by weeks of cold, unsettled weather. Remarkably, every single one of the last 28 days has been anomalously cold across this region - a full rolling month of below-normal temperatures that climate scientists say is now shaping a sharply different autumn for central Mexico.

beats.title: Cold Front No. 8 triggers Mexico's most intense autumn storm in living memory
beats.text: Cold Front No. 8, driven by a polar trough interacting with both the polar and subtropical jet streams, began sweeping across north-western Mexico on 26 November and is now tracking through the country's western and central states. CONAGUA's weather advisory warns of potential snow and sleet overnight in the mountainous areas of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacán, with temperatures falling to between -5 °C and 0 °C with frost even in valleys. Torrential rain is forecast in Michoacán and Guerrero today, with intense rainfall affecting Sinaloa, Nayarit, Jalisco and Guanajuato.

beats.title: 28 consecutive cold days - an entire month of anomalous chill
beats.text: The ERA5 statistics reveal extraordinary persistence: every one of the last 28 days has been anomalously cold at the ERA5 focus point in western Mexico. The 28-day rainfall total of 18.2 mm is well below the expected 9.8 mm per 14-day period, confirming dominance by dry, cold Arctic air rather than the moist tropical conditions normal for late November. This is by some margin the longest unbroken cold anomaly recorded in this region at this time of year in the full ERA5 archive.

beats.title: #1 in 87 years: Mexico's most extreme November cold anomaly
beats.text: The cold anomaly of -8.3 °C relative to the 1991-2020 seasonal norm of +19.6 °C places this event at the 99.4th percentile of ERA5 records for this date - ranked first in 87 years of data back to 1940. This is unprecedented in the full ERA5 record for this location on this calendar date. Even accounting for the natural variability of winter cold-air outbreaks, no comparable event has been recorded here at this time of year in the modern reanalysis era.

beats.title: A warming Mexico makes Arctic cold outbreaks even more shocking by contrast
beats.text: Local seasonal warming of +1.19 °C since the 1940-1979 baseline means that background temperatures across western Mexico are now considerably warmer than they were in the mid-20th century. When rare deep Arctic air outbreaks do penetrate this far south, they therefore create a more extreme contrast with the warm baseline, producing the kind of record-breaking anomalies seen today. The frequency of p90 cold exceedances has edged down slightly - from five to three per season in recent decades - but those that do occur are intensified by the sharp contrast with an otherwise warming climate.

stories.headline: Sumatra flood crisis deepens as 1,190 homes swept away in 162 mm deluge
stories.ticker: **Indonesia's Sumatra island** is reeling from its most intense November rainfall in modern records: **162.8 mm in 24 hours** at the ECMWF focus point ranks **unprecedented - #1 in 87 years since 1940** against a seasonal norm of just 11.8 mm. /// On **25 November**, the Batang Tapan River in **West Sumatra's Pesisir Selatan district** burst its banks, destroying **at least 1,190 homes** and cutting off road access to four villages. /// Across the broader archipelago, **floods, landslides and strong winds have struck 8 provinces since 17 November** - from North Sumatra to Central Sulawesi. /// The **14-day rainfall total stands at 191.4 mm**, more than 32 times the expected 5.9 mm, confirming **7 of 14 days have been anomalously wet**. /// Deforestation across millions of hectares in Sumatra and a **local warming of +0.56 °C since the 1940s** are turning every monsoon surge into a catastrophic flash-flood event.
stories.voice_script: In Indonesia's Sumatra, North Sumatra and Aceh have been battered by the heaviest November rains since records began, with 162.8 millimetres falling in a single 24-hour period - ranked number one in 87 years. On 25 November, the Batang Tapan River in West Sumatra's Pesisir Selatan regency burst its banks, destroying at least 1,190 homes, one health facility and cutting road access to four villages. Indonesia's national disaster agency BNPB confirms floods, landslides and strong winds have struck eight provinces stretching from North Sumatra to Central Sulawesi since 17 November, affecting tens of thousands of residents. Over the past 14 days, 191.4 millimetres of rain has accumulated across South Sumatra - more than 32 times the climatological norm of 5.9 millimetres per fortnight, with 7 of those 14 days recording anomalously extreme rainfall. Decades of deforestation across millions of hectares in Sumatra, combined with sea-surface warming of more than half a degree since the 1940s, are systematically converting monsoon rainfall into catastrophic flash floods and landslides.

beats.title: 1,190 homes destroyed in West Sumatra as river bursts its banks
beats.text: Indonesia's National Disaster Management Agency BNPB confirmed on 26 November that the Batang Tapan River in Pesisir Selatan Regency, West Sumatra, overflowed on the afternoon of 25 November after intense upstream rainfall, destroying at least 1,190 homes across four villages in Ranah Ampek Hulu Tapan sub-district. One health facility and a road were also destroyed, cutting off communities. A rapid-response team is operating from a command post in Tapan. The broader disaster picture now spans eight provinces from North Sumatra to Central Sulawesi.

beats.title: Seven anomalous rain days in a fortnight - soils fully saturated
beats.text: ERA5 persistence data shows that 7 of the last 14 days have been anomalously wet at the ECMWF model focus point off the southern Sumatran coast. The 14-day rainfall accumulation of 191.4 mm is more than 32 times the climatological expectation of 5.9 mm for the same period. The 28-day total stands at 225.6 mm. This relentless saturation of soils and swelling of rivers means that even moderate further rainfall is now capable of triggering flash flooding and landslides across the entire island.

beats.title: #1 in 87 years: the most extreme November daily rainfall on record for Sumatra
beats.text: The 24-hour rainfall total of 162.8 mm is ranked first in ERA5 records extending from 1940 to the present - 87 years of data - for this precise calendar date at this Sumatran focus point. The seasonal climatological norm is just 11.8 mm per day, placing this event at the 99.4th percentile of the full ERA5 distribution. Indonesia's meteorological agency BMKG had already placed North Sumatra under its highest-level 'Awas' alert for extreme rainfall, with weather-modification cloud-seeding operations deployed in an attempt to reduce peak rain intensities.

beats.title: Warming seas and forest loss are amplifying every Sumatra flood event
beats.text: Local seasonal warming of +0.56 °C since the 1940-1979 period has modestly increased background sea-surface temperatures in the waters off Sumatra, feeding additional moisture into every convective event. More critically, the frequency of p90 extreme-rain days has tripled - from 2 occurrences per season in the pre-warming era to 6 in the modern period (1986-2025). Compounding this, as research on the 2025 Southeast Asia floods confirmed, the loss of millions of hectares of Sumatran forest over the past two decades has eliminated the natural water retention and absorption systems, converting heavy rain into deadly flash floods and landslides with ever-greater efficiency.

stories.kicker: GLOBAL HEAT RECORD · EAST SIBERIA, RUSSIA
stories.headline: Yakutia shatters all records as a +23 °C anomaly grips the Arctic fringe
stories.ticker: **Russia's East Siberia** - the coldest inhabited region on Earth - is experiencing a temperature anomaly of **+23.0 °C above the late-November norm** of -25 °C, with the actual air temperature at just **-5.1 °C where -28 °C is climatologically normal**. /// This is **unprecedented - ranked #1 in 87 years since 1940**, sitting at the **99.4th percentile** of the full ERA5 archive. /// Over the past **28 days, 22 have been anomalously warm**, with no break in the persistent ridge that has suppressed the polar cold throughout. /// Since the **1940-1979 baseline, local warming here has reached +1.59 °C**, and the number of **extreme warm-anomaly days has surged from zero to nine per season** - a transformation with no historical parallel in the region's records. /// As the global mean anomaly flirts with **record 2 °C+ above pre-industrial levels**, East Siberia is ground zero for the most dramatic signal yet seen.
stories.voice_script: In Russia's East Siberia, the city of Yakutsk - famed as the coldest city on Earth - is recording temperatures 23 degrees above normal, the most extraordinary warm anomaly here in 87 years of records. At Verkhoyansk, where temperatures typically plunge to minus 25 Celsius by late November, the thermometer stands at a barely frosty minus 5 - a gap of 20 degrees from what any historical analogue would expect. Twenty-two of the last 28 days have been anomalously warm across Arctic Yakutia, confirming that this is not a brief spike but a prolonged and deeply embedded atmospheric pattern of historic scale. A persistent high-pressure ridge over the Laptev Sea at 995 hectopascals has suppressed the normal southward drainage of Arctic cold, trapping warm Atlantic air over East Siberia for most of November. Climate data shows local warming of 1.59 degrees since the 1940s has driven p90 extreme warm-day events from zero to nine per season in this region - a region that once recorded the coldest temperatures outside Antarctica is now a frontline of rapid Arctic warming.

beats.title: Earth's coldest city records a barely frosty -5 °C in deep November
beats.text: Yakutsk, the administrative capital of Russia's Sakha Republic and widely regarded as the coldest city on Earth, is today recording an air temperature of approximately -5 °C. By late November, the city typically sits at around -25 °C, with nights far colder. The 20-degree departure from normal is being driven by a persistent blocking ridge over the Laptev Sea that has suppressed the normal southward flow of Arctic air and allowed warm Atlantic influence to penetrate all the way to the Pacific-facing side of the continent.

beats.title: 22 of 28 days anomalously warm - three weeks of unbroken Arctic heat
beats.text: ERA5 persistence data shows that 22 of the last 28 days have been anomalously warm at the East Siberia focus point (71.0 °N, 144.5 °E), and 9 of the last 14 days have continued the pattern. The 28-day rainfall total of 29.0 mm is nearly six times the climatological expectation of 5.0 mm for the period, indicating that unusually moist mild air has dominated. This is a remarkable and prolonged atmospheric state: in a region built around the most extreme cold on the planet, three consecutive weeks of anomalous warmth constitute a genuinely historic event.

beats.title: #1 in 87 years: East Siberia's greatest ever November warm anomaly
beats.text: The temperature anomaly of +23.0 °C ranks first in ERA5 records for this calendar date stretching back 87 years to 1940, placing it at the 99.4th percentile - the top of the entire distribution. The seasonal climatological norm here is -25.0 °C. This anomaly is unprecedented in the full reanalysis record. It coincides with the period of globally record-breaking daily temperature anomalies logged by the Copernicus Climate Change Service in late November 2026, when the global mean anomaly briefly reached +2.23 °C above pre-industrial levels.

beats.title: From zero to nine: extreme warm days surge as the Arctic amplifies
beats.text: The climate change signal in East Siberia is among the most dramatic anywhere on Earth. Local seasonal warming of +1.59 °C since the 1940-1979 baseline period has fundamentally altered the region's temperature regime. Most strikingly, the number of days per season exceeding the 90th percentile warm threshold has surged from zero in the pre-warming era (1940-1979) to nine in the modern period (1986-2025) - a transformation from no extreme warm days at all to near-weekly occurrences. Arctic amplification - the well-documented tendency for the Arctic to warm roughly four times faster than the global mean - is the primary mechanism, weakening the polar vortex and enabling warm air intrusions of precisely this type.
